title: The Trump Administration Keeps Ghosting Its Congressional Watchdog - NOTUS
description:
A growing number of federal agencies are either refusing to provide the Government Accountability Office access to information or ignoring the congressional watchdog altogether.
OMB sent a particularly harsh letter to the GAO — and published it— when the watchdog agency started to investigate whether the Trump administration was abiding by the 1974 Impoundment Control Act in its rush to dismantle USAID.
GAO insiders told NOTUS that executive agencies are naturally wary of outside inspectors.
Federal agencies rarely turn over personnel data, even though government employees’ salaries are generally presumed to be a matter of public record.
None of the 12 generals, admirals or DOD civilian leaders would talk to the congressional watchdog agency.
text:
A growing number of federal agencies are either refusing to provide the Government Accountability Office access to information or ignoring the congressional watchdog altogether.

Agencies have been stonewalling the GAO ever since President Donald Trump returned to office, to the point that GAO leadership told employees at a staff meeting in May that they’ve encountered “significant access issues” during the last year and a half, according to two sources familiar with the event and confirmed by GAO. Officials at that meeting cited the Office of Management and Budget, Housing and Urban Development, the Commerce Department, the Education Department and the Small Business Administration as particularly noncooperative.

None of those executive agencies responded to detailed questions this week about whether they are purposefully hindering oversight or the nature of their interactions with the legislative agency whose mission is to monitor government operations and identify waste, fraud and abuse.

During the May meeting, GAO general counsel Edda Emmanuelli Perez told employees “there have been some outright denials,” sometimes from federal agencies who claim GAO lacks authority because the request came from a ranking member — which at the moment, means Democrats. In some cases, the office has been denied records and data it had received without any issues in the past.

Trending

In an interview last week, she told NOTUS that while the agency was encountering “access issues,” it was “working them through.”

It’s no surprise that the OMB is on the short list of federal agencies refusing to cooperate with the GAO. Russell Vought, OMB’s director, has made it his mission to expand presidential power over government agencies. OMB sent a particularly harsh letter to the GAO — and published it— when the watchdog agency started to investigate whether the Trump administration was abiding by the 1974 Impoundment Control Act in its rush to dismantle USAID. Mark Paoletta, the government-gutting lawyer Trump once deemed a “conservative warrior” who was then serving as OMB’s general counsel, chided the GAO’s requests as “voluminous, burdensome, and inappropriately invasive.”

Paoletta went on to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, where he sent another bellicose letter to the GAO when auditors explored whether CFPB could legitimately fulfill its legally mandated function as the Trump administration fired scores of its workforce. Paoletta railed against what he called GAO’s “arbitrary deadlines” and derided the group’s work as nothing more than an “incomplete” exercise “initiated at the behest of hyper-partisan Democrat members.”

The GAO study into CFPB had been requested by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking member on the Senate banking committee, House Financial Services Committee Chair Maxine Waters and three other Democrats. In that study, GAO analysts described how the agency’s refusal to cooperate during much of 2025 forced them to look for answers by scouring public court filings in a CFPB lawsuit, Federal Register notices and even press releases — meaning it had about as much access to information as the average person with a computer.

“Stonewalling a nonpartisan congressional watchdog is another way that President Trump is trying to keep Congress and the American public in the dark about how his policies are hurting American families,” Warren said in a statement to NOTUS. “Congress should start sending subpoenas if the Trump administration won’t cooperate with legitimate oversight.”

In other instances, agencies have not responded to GAO’s emailed questions or even acknowledged that an audit is taking place. At the staff meeting last month, GAO leadership told analysts and directors who conduct those probes to consider accommodating reluctant federal agencies — for example, by narrowing requests — but to keep track of deadlines so that if agencies fail to respond, they can loop in supervisors or even members of Congress to apply pressure to those agencies. One GAO source pointed to an executive branch agency closely controlled by the Trump White House that has not participated at all in an ongoing audit that began last year — denying analysts even basic interviews to explain certain government operations under review.

And analysts are frustrated that longer delays make every “engagement,” as they’re referred to by the GAO, more expensive.

Liz Hempowicz, the deputy executive director of the government accountability nonprofit American Oversight, said she hadn’t heard that federal agencies were pushing back on GAO audits on partisan grounds, but she called the pushback “alarming.” She ascribed it to Republicans uniformly falling in line behind Trump on most issues, leading to tepid congressional oversight.

“Both GAO and these agencies are entities of the government meant to serve the American people. A ranking member represents a constituency of the American people the same way that a chair does. Treating that distinction as the be-all, end-all is just so insulting,” she said.

Janice Luong, a policy analyst at the nonprofit Project On Government Oversight said Congress needs to step in, particularly as the Trump administration consolidates power in the executive branch and chips away at Congress’ power of the purse.

“Congress should most definitely speak up and defend GAO and the legislative agency that provides them with resources on how dollars are spent — and holding the executive branch accountable,” she told NOTUS.

Some signs of the rising tensions have occasionally slipped into public view, but they’ve mostly been buried deep in monotonous congressional hearings or vaguely described in official reports.

In December, the previous head of the GAO, who retired when his 15-year tenure reached its statutory end, told a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subcommittee that “at this point, OMB’s not cooperating as much as we had in the past.”

“We used to have, you know, meetings with them,” then-Comptroller General Gene Dodaro said. “That’s not happening. I think it’s unfortunate because they can benefit from continued dialogue with us.”

The GAO has always run into some bureaucratic resistance from executive agencies when attempting to review government programs, no matter which political party is in the White House — a point agency officials emphasized to NOTUS.

The GAO’s annual report in 2024 said the Biden administration’s Department of Education had “regularly delayed providing information to which GAO has statutory access.” The agency had to get members of Congress to intervene. In the end, GAO analysts exposed errors that resulted in 432,000 fewer people — mostly prospective college students from poorer families — submitting a FAFSA, or Free Application for Federal Student Aid. In one case, the government website instructed people to dial “7” for translation services, but that option didn’t exist on a call.

GAO insiders told NOTUS that executive agencies are naturally wary of outside inspectors. Spy agencies and the military are notoriously guarded. Federal agencies rarely turn over personnel data, even though government employees’ salaries are generally presumed to be a matter of public record.

From July 2024 to May 2025, the GAO looked into the consequences of Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville’s 11-month “blanket hold” on all senior military promotions during the Biden administration. Analysts concluded the blockade didn’t actually affect combat readiness — but they had to rely partly on public statements from Defense Department brass. None of the 12 generals, admirals or DOD civilian leaders would talk to the congressional watchdog agency.

The GAO is a legislative agency that belongs entirely to Congress and thus lies beyond Trump’s reach. When DOGE came knocking last year, NOTUS broke the news that GAO leadership rallied the troops with an email that reminded employees “we are not subject to DOGE or executive orders.”

In an interview last Friday, Emmanuelli Perez, the GAO general counsel, acknowledged some recent obstacles and pointed to what the agency had said in its year-end performance and accountability reports, the latest of which says, in government speak, that “FY 2025 was different.”

“We were seeing more delays. So we were saying, ‘OK, it’s getting really slow and that is having an impact.’ We saw that there is some information we routinely obtained in the past that now was either slowed down or we were having more trouble getting,” she told NOTUS.

name: Human Rights
title: Just 3% of recent ICE detainees had a violent felony conviction, government data shows
authors: Maggie Green, Laura Romero, Matt Rivers, ABC News
description:
The most detainees under the previous administration was 39,748 in November 2023, according to a nonprofit data gathering group.
The data also showed that in the first eight months of 2025, ICE apprehended the parents of approximately 14,450 U.S.-born children.
And of the more than 6,400 detained parents, 322 had a violent felony conviction.
The Deportation Data Project provides minimally processed and unprocessed data supplied to them directly by ICE via FOIA.
Methodology ABC News analyzed enforcement trends by merging two primary sources: data provided by ICE via FOIA requests to the Deportation Data Project and ICE data provided to the University of Washington Center for Human Rights.
text:
Only 3% of individuals detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during the first 14 months of the second Trump administration had a violent felony conviction, according to an ABC News analysis of government data.

The findings, based on data tracking the current Trump administration's immigration crackdown, come after President Donald Trump had pledged to target the "worst of the worst" criminal offenders among the nation's migrants.

Based on government data analyzed by ABC News as provided by ICE in response to a FOIA requests to the Deportation Data Project and the University of Washington Center for Human Rights, the findings show that immigration enforcement has affected more than 400,000 individuals with no violent criminal history, including parents and spouses of U.S. citizens.

While the 3% figure is consistent with rates seen under the Biden administration, the data shows the Trump administration is not detaining a higher proportion of violent offenders despite a significant overall increase in total detentions.

'President Trump's promise'

Under Trump, there has been record high detention population, currently at around 60,000 in federal immigration custody. The most detainees under the previous administration was 39,748 in November 2023, according to a nonprofit data gathering group.

According to the government data, of the 438,537 people detained between Jan. 20, 2025, and March 11, 2026, 13,018 had a violent felony conviction in the United States. The analysis defined "violent felony" as homicide, sexual assault, robbery, or assault.

The data also showed that in the first eight months of 2025, ICE apprehended the parents of approximately 14,450 U.S.-born children. This eight-month figure nearly surpassed the total for all of 2024 and surpassed the yearly totals for both 2022 and 2023.

Of those apprehended during the administration's first seven months, more than 9,700 children saw at least one parent placed into immigration detention -- more than in previous years. Of those detained, parents of more than 7,000 children were eventually deported. Of the more than 4,700 deported parents, 265 had a violent felony conviction. And of the more than 6,400 detained parents, 322 had a violent felony conviction.

In a statement to ABC News, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said, "Since Day One, DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump's promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists. This data is being cherry picked by the Deportation Data Project to peddle a false narrative."

The Deportation Data Project provides minimally processed and unprocessed data supplied to them directly by ICE via FOIA.

"Nearly 70% of ICE arrests are criminal illegal aliens," the statement went on to say. "We are continuing to go after the worst of the worst -- including gang members, pedophiles, and rapists. Many of the individuals that are counted as 'non-criminals' are actually terrorists, human rights abusers, gangsters and more; they just don't have a rap sheet in the U.S."

"Further, every single one of these individuals committed a crime when they came into this country illegally," the statement said regarding charges of unlawful entry, which is generally a civil violation, not a criminal offense.

'Economic consequences'

Andrea Flores, the founder of Securing America's Promise and a former Department of Homeland Security official, said the policy of mass deportation could lead to a child welfare crisis.

"So many children are losing primary caretakers or going to guardians," Flores said in a Zoom interview. "We are going to have a class of children who lose their parents under this administration that is bigger than we probably have seen in modern history."

DHS said in a statement that ICE does not separate families and that "parents are asked if they want to be removed with their children or ICE will place the children with a safe person the parent designates."

In the first eight months of 2025, ICE also apprehended 4,843 spouses of U.S. citizens. During the first seven months of the term, more than 2,000 of these spouses were deported. Of the more than 2,000 spouses of U.S. citizens deported during the first seven months of the term, 165 had a violent felony conviction.

"We cannot underplay what it means to have even just a spouse go to detention, because what if they are the primary earner in that household?" Flores said. "We're talking about economic consequences. We're talking about the emotional costs of not having access to that family member."

Trump administration officials have said that its crackdown on illegal immigration is primarily targeting dangerous and violent criminals living in the U.S. illegally, but they have also maintained that anyone residing in the country without legal status is subject to removal.

Methodology

ABC News analyzed enforcement trends by merging two primary sources: data provided by ICE via FOIA requests to the Deportation Data Project and ICE data provided to the University of Washington Center for Human Rights. The data provided to the Deportation Data Project includes data from the Department of Homeland Security's PERSIST database, which shows the full lifecycle of immigration cases from January 2022 through early March 2026.

The data provided to the University of Washington Center for Human Rights includes I-213 records, which are the documents created when immigration officers arrest a noncitizen. These records span from January 2022 through late August 2025.

Publicly available data from ICE and DHS show detention populations and numbers on removals.

Statistics regarding the total number of parents and spouses apprehended were calculated using the University of Washington dataset alone. To determine how many of those individuals were specifically detained or deported, ABC News matched records across both databases using unique identifiers such as the date of arrest, gender, country of citizenship, and birth year.

The analysis focused on a subset of the data where a definitive match could be made between the two sources. The merged dataset allowed ABC News to track the progression of individual cases from the initial arrest through federal custody to identify parents and spouses who were ultimately held in facilities or removed from the country.

ABC News' estimates for the number of U.S. citizens who had a parent or spouse arrested, detained and deported are likely an undercount. ProPublica, a nonprofit news organization, first reported similar data in March.

ABC News' analysis of U.S. citizens who had a parent or spouse detained is limited to only individuals for whom arresting agents wrote an I-213 report, which represents the vast majority of individuals arrested by ICE, but is not everyone who has been detained. To perform the analysis, any possible duplicates in the data were not counted.

Flores said these numbers will likely grow.

"We have seen some recent reporting as well that the numbers are going into the tens of thousands in terms of children who have been impacted by a detained parent," Flores said. "There are 4 million U.S. citizen children in current estimates who have a parent that isn't documented."

ABC News' Ryann Jones and Armando Garcia contributed to this report.

name: Litigation
title: Florida's failed lawsuit over immigrant truckers was actually a win - Palm Beach Daily News
description:
Florida's lawsuit stemmed from a fatal crash involving an immigrant driver who was issued licenses by the two states.
According to the State of Florida's lawsuit against California and Washington, "State and federal investigations revealed that the illegal immigrant does not speak English.
"The Supreme Court didn't give a reason for its May 26 denial, which is standard practice in such situations," noted Aronberg.
Pannun praised the Supreme Court decision as "a victory for the rule of law" that "protects thousands of hard-working truck drivers across America.
"The administrative process worked exactly the way it was supposed to, rendering Florida's lawsuit completely obsolete," said Aronberg.
text:
The Supreme Court denied Florida's attempt to sue California and Washington over their commercial driver's licensing programs.

Legal experts suggest a ruling in Florida's favor could have exposed it to lawsuits over its own policies and licensing issues.

Florida's lawsuit stemmed from a fatal crash involving an immigrant driver who was issued licenses by the two states.

New federal rules now limit which non-citizens can obtain commercial driver's licenses, addressing the core issue of Florida's suit.

The state of Florida failed in its attempt to use last year's fatal truck crash on Florida's Turnpike to compel the Supreme Court to crack down on California's and Washington state's commercial driver's licensing programs.

That was a blessing in disguise for Florida, legal experts say.

Had Florida State Attorney General James Uthmeier prevailed in pinning the blame on the two sanctuary states that issued commercial driver's licenses to the immigrant driver accused of causing the accident, it would have opened the door for other states — including California and Washington — to sue Florida over a wide range of issues including its policies regarding firearms and vaccinations.

Florida could even have been sued for its own improper issuing of commercial driver's licenses to immigrants with a limited ability to read and speak English.

That's because of multiple instances in recent years where the Florida Department of Motor Vehicles issued CDLs to immigrant drivers who went on to cause fatal truck crashes in other states and were subsequently found unable to sufficiently read and speak English, according to Washington state's legal response to the Supreme Court.

Then there's the two massive CDL fraud schemes in Florida uncovered last year:

One involved state DMV employees in Bay County who took bribes in exchange for issuing CDLs to immigrant applicants without requiring them to take driving skills or English language proficiency tests.

A second was in Jacksonville where applicants were allowed to take tests while wearing communication devices where they were supplied answers in their native tongue.

Florida also consistently ranks third in the nation each year for most fatal truck crashes, including 211 last year that resulted in 234 deaths, according to Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration data. Only Texas (519 crashes causing 580 deaths) and California (247 crashes causing 275 deaths) had more.

States suing each other would 'overwhelm Supreme Court's docket'

"If the Supreme Court opened the door for states to sue each other over poorly administered CDL programs, Florida would be a prime target," said Dave Aronberg, a former Florida state attorney who now manages his own law practice, Dave Aronberg Law P.A., in West Palm Beach. He added, "Trying to use the original jurisdiction of the U.S. Supreme Court to micro-manage the DMV (Department of Motor Vehicle) processes of states thousands of miles away was a legal longshot from Day One."

Louis "Lou" Virelli III, a professor at Stetson University's College of Law in St. Petersburg, came to the same conclusion. "The Supreme Court's docket could be overwhelmed by states suing each other for their policy choices," he said, adding that the high court's 7-2 decision to deny Florida's complaint was "not on the merits, but based on the court's discretionary jurisdiction." Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito cast the two dissenting votes.

Jae Williams, press secretary for the Florida Attorney General's office, issued the following written statement to USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA in response to the Supreme Court's decision: "Unfortunately, the Supreme Court leaves Floridians with no avenue to hold California accountable for putting dangerous, illegal alien truck drivers on our roads, despite the U.S. Constitution's mandate and Congress directing the Court to hear controversies between the states."

The Florida Attorney General's office did not respond to requests for further comment.

Why did Florida go to the Supreme Court to sue California and Washington?

Florida's lawsuit against California and Washington had to do with the two states issuing CDLs to Harjinder Singh, the illegal immigrant truck driver accused of causing the fatal truck crash on Aug. 12, 2025 that killed three people when when he made an illegal U-turn on a crossover marked "Official Use Only" along the Florida's Turnpike near Fort Pierce.

The three Florida residents were killed when the minivan they were riding in collided with Singh's 18-wheel semi-trailer as it was making its U-turn. The Official Use Only sign was accompanied by a universal "No U-turn" symbol.

Singh, 28, is a native of north India of Sikh heritage who entered the United States illegally in 2018 and was issued a CDL from Washington state in 2023 and a non-domiciled CDL from California in 2024. He lives in California.

According to the State of Florida's lawsuit against California and Washington, "State and federal investigations revealed that the illegal immigrant does not speak English. He was able to answer only two of 12 questions correctly on an English proficiency test and identify only one of four traffic signs."

Florida's lawsuit blamed the issuance of CDLs to Singh by California and Washington as resulting in "increasing inspections at state entry points, adding to the workload of both state police and agricultural law enforcement officers."

The lawsuit also urged the Supreme Court to preempt California and Washington's sanctuary laws, which it claimed "prohibit agencies administering CDL programs from inquiring into or collecting information about an applicant's immigration status," as well as to ban the two states from issuing CDLs to applicants who are not U.S. citizens or permanent residents.

Florida in its lawsuit stated that it was presenting its case against California and Washington to the Supreme Court because "no other adequate forum is available for this dispute between separate sovereigns."

In a somewhat unusual move, Uthmeier announced the filing of the lawsuit against California and Washington on the "Hannity" political talk show on Fox News as opposed to the traditional method of holding a press conference.

How did California and Washington react about the claims in Florida's lawsuit?

California and Washington in their legal responses to the Supreme Court both called Florida's lawsuit "unserious" because it failed to show how the their respective CDL programs directly caused the fatal truck crash involving Singh.

Both states also maintained that they follow federal regulations in issuing CDLs, including requiring the ability to read and speak English at a level sufficient to safely operate a commercial vehicle.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, in his state's legal response, disputed Florida's claim that the Supreme Court was the only available venue to address the matter.

"Florida's complaint focuses on a single car accident — a classic kind of personal injury that private plaintiffs can redress," he wrote. "And any concerns about compliance with federal law can be, and already being, addressed by the FMCSA's review process."

Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown's response to Florida's lawsuit included stating that "Washington law requires CDL applicants to pass written knowledge tests and skills that meet federal standards and prohibits issuance of a CDL unless the applicant is domiciled in Washington and otherwise federally qualified."

Brown added: "Florida lacks standing because it has failed to show an actual harm directly caused by Washington or a remedy this Court could provide that would redress the harm Florida alleges."

Washington state's response to the Supreme Court also listed several instances in which Florida improperly issued CDLs to immigrants with limited English language skills who went on to cause fatal truck crashes.

"The Supreme Court didn't give a reason for its May 26 denial, which is standard practice in such situations," noted Aronberg. "However, Washington's response raised an uncomfortable truth: Florida lives in a glass house on this issue."

California and Washington did revoke CDLs to some immigrants

While California and Washington insist they follow federal standards in issuing CDLs, both states recently canceled a number of licenses issued to immigrants in recent years.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles on March 6 canceled 13,000 non-domiciled CDLs effective immediately per a federal government mandate.

Non-domiciled individuals are those who do not have citizenship or lawful permanent resident status and includes holders of various visas, refugees and asylum seekers.

The California DMV in its press release announcing the cancellations stated that the non-domiciled CDL holders whose licenses got revoked were legally present in the U.S. and met language and safety rules when the licenses were issued.

Washington state's Department of Licensing in December revoked 685 standard CDLs that it acknowledged were issued in error to noncitizens between 2018 and 2025. It also announced a temporary halt in issuing non-domiciled CDLs.

"Errors have been addressed, and DOL is working to make changes in our system ... to prevent mis-issuances in the future," Washington state DOL spokesman Nathan Olson told the regional news website Source One in a Dec. 9 article.

Why are there so many Sikh truckers in the U.S. (including Florida)?

According to some estimates, including The Economist and the India-based news website Firstpost, the number of Sikh truckers in the U.S. may be as many as 135,000 to 150,000.

Gurpatwant Pannun, general counsel for the New York-based Sikhs for Justice organization, believes the number of Sikh truckers in the U.S. is more than 100,000, including "between 3,000 and 5,000" in Florida.

Some are refugees who fled their native homeland in the Punjab region that bisects India and Pakistan to escape religious persecution.

The reason many Sikhs become truckers in the U.S. is because "it allows for entrepreneurial independence while offering flexibility to observe our religious articles of faith, including the turban and beard," wrote Pannun in an email to USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA.

What is Sikhism?

Sikhism is the world's fifth largest organized religion with over 27 million adherents, including an estimated 750,000 in the U.S., according to the New York-based Sikh Coalition. The group states that its religion's core values are love, service and justice and that its followers are easily distinguishable by their uncut hair and wearing of turbans by males.

It is also a religion that is separate from Hinduism and Islam (the dominant religions of India and Pakistan, respectively), with its own places of worship that are called a Gurdwara, or "door of the guru."

Why did Sikhs gather outside a Florida jail?

A small gathering of members of Sikhs for Justice on Aug. 28, 2025 held a "peaceful prayer vigil" outside the St. Lucie County jail where Singh is being held following last year's fatal truck crash.

Pannun who took part in the vigil said it was held to express "deep condolences to the families of the victims," raise funds for the victims' funerals, while "simultaneously standing up" for Harjinder Singh's right to due process.

"Our message is very clear: everyone must get a fair trial," wrote Pannun. "The tragic crash involving Harjinder Singh was an individual case that is currently going through the legal system. It should not be weaponized to restrict industry access (to Sikhs) or to stoke anti-immigrant sentiment."

Pannun added that his organization "supports any legitimate, non-discriminatory measure that improves highway safety for everyone."

That includes the longstanding federal law requiring all CDL holders to have "a working command of the English language," he wrote. "This is not a profession where you can simply bypass safety standards. The reason so many Sikhs enter trucking is due to a strong cultural work ethic, a robust community mentorship network, and the opportunity for economic upward mobility — not a lack of regulations."

How did truckers, Sikh groups react to the Supreme Court's decision?

Armando Reynaldo is an independent trucker based in Hernando County. He doesn't know what to make of the Supreme Court's decision, but agrees something needs to be done to crack down on immigrant truckers who "don't speak English and don't care."

"I know a lot of people who don't speak English good but they understand the laws," said Reynaldo, himself an immigrant from Cuba.

Unfortunately, that's not the case for all immigrant truckers, he said. "I don't know how they got their license. They are a danger. Even in a truck stop, they don't know how to back up their truck. A lot are good, but there's a lot that don't need to be in a truck."

Lewie Pugh is executive vice president of the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association based in the Kansas City, Missouri area. The OOIDA represents more than 150,000 truckers across the U.S. and Canada, including some who are Sikh.

Pugh understands why the Supreme Court elected to not hear Florida's lawsuit against California and Washington. "Florida was trying to fix this in the courts. We feel it's better addressed by the FMCSA (Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration)," he said.

The OOIDA is pushing to establish higher nationwide standards for obtaining a CDL that includes a minimum of 30 hours of behind-the-wheel training, a requirement to read and speak English without the help of a translator, and doing away with non-domiciled CDL programs that allow drivers to train outside their home state and receive a commercial license in a state other than the one they primarily reside in, according to Josh Klein, the association's deputy communications director.

"We are primarily push for these changes through regulations and legislation rather than through the courts," said Pugh.

Pannun praised the Supreme Court decision as "a victory for the rule of law" that "protects thousands of hard-working truck drivers across America. The Court has ensured that states like California and Washington cannot have their licensing systems upended based on a single tragic accident."

Graham West, a spokesman for the New York-based Sikh Coalition, also praised the Supreme Court's decision, but did not characterize it as a victory.

"A successful lawsuit could have had a chilling effect in the willingness of states cross the nation to issue non-domiciled commercial driver's licenses to qualified and lawfully present drivers," he told USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA in an email. "More broadly however, the larger point is somewhat moot given that FMCSA's Final Rule barring most categories of immigrants from obtaining or renewing non-domiciled CDLs is in effect and won't hear its next legal challenge until September."

West was referring to new nationwide FMCSA regulations that took effect March 16.

How the fed's new 'Final Rule' for CDLs accomplishes the aim of Florida's suit

The FMCSA's so-called "Final Rule" limits those eligible to receive a CDL to U.S. citizens and immigrants who are either permanent residents or who hold an H-2A (agricultural worker), H-2B (seasonal non-agricultural worker) or E-2 (treaty investor nation) visa.

No longer eligible are recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) status, refugees and asylum seekers.

"The scope of that exclusion is substantial," according to a March 10 article in the supply chain, transportation and logistics industry trade publication FreightWaves. "FMCSA estimates that 97% of the current 200,000 non-domiciled CDL holders nationwide will not be able to satisfy the new requirements under the Final Rule, assuming it survives legal challenge."

If allowed to stand, the Final Rule could see between 214,000 and 437,000 truckers removed from the workforce nationally over the next two to three years, according to an analysis by Arkansas-based trucking giant J.B. Hunt Transport Services, the FreightWaves article stated.

The Final Rule is being challenged in court by the AFL-CIO, American Federation of Teachers and Public Citizens, the Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit consumer advocacy group founded by Ralph Nader.

"The administrative process worked exactly the way it was supposed to, rendering Florida's lawsuit completely obsolete," said Aronberg. "The federal government has stepped in and is attempting to solve the core safety gap.

"It seems good public policy to have a centralized federal standard that ensures that anyone behind the wheel of an 80,000-pound rig has had their background and driving competency thoroughly vetted. Public safety should always be the primary concern."

Clayton Park is a journalist for the USA TODAY NETWORK FLORIDA. He covers everything from insurance, utilities and home prices to groceries, gas and auto prices as the Florida consumer pocketbook reporter. text:
The Supreme Court denied Florida's attempt to sue California and Washington over their commercial driver's licensing programs.

Legal experts suggest a ruling in Florida's favor could have exposed it to lawsuits over its own policies and licensing issues.

Florida's lawsuit stemmed from a fatal crash involving an immigrant driver who was issued licenses by the two states.

New federal rules now limit which non-citizens can obtain commercial driver's licenses, addressing the core issue of Florida's suit.

The state of Florida failed in its attempt to use last year's fatal truck crash on Florida's Turnpike to compel the Supreme Court to crack down on California's and Washington state's commercial driver's licensing programs.

That was a blessing in disguise for Florida, legal experts say.

Had Florida State Attorney General James Uthmeier prevailed in pinning the blame on the two sanctuary states that issued commercial driver's licenses to the immigrant driver accused of causing the accident, it would have opened the door for other states — including California and Washington — to sue Florida over a wide range of issues including its policies regarding firearms and vaccinations.

Florida could even have been sued for its own improper issuing of commercial driver's licenses to immigrants with a limited ability to read and speak English.

That's because of multiple instances in recent years where the Florida Department of Motor Vehicles issued CDLs to immigrant drivers who went on to cause fatal truck crashes in other states and were subsequently found unable to sufficiently read and speak English, according to Washington state's legal response to the Supreme Court.

Then there's the two massive CDL fraud schemes in Florida uncovered last year:

One involved state DMV employees in Bay County who took bribes in exchange for issuing CDLs to immigrant applicants without requiring them to take driving skills or English language proficiency tests.

A second was in Jacksonville where applicants were allowed to take tests while wearing communication devices where they were supplied answers in their native tongue.

Florida also consistently ranks third in the nation each year for most fatal truck crashes, including 211 last year that resulted in 234 deaths, according to Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration data. Only Texas (519 crashes causing 580 deaths) and California (247 crashes causing 275 deaths) had more.

States suing each other would 'overwhelm Supreme Court's docket'

"If the Supreme Court opened the door for states to sue each other over poorly administered CDL programs, Florida would be a prime target," said Dave Aronberg, a former Florida state attorney who now manages his own law practice, Dave Aronberg Law P.A., in West Palm Beach. He added, "Trying to use the original jurisdiction of the U.S. Supreme Court to micro-manage the DMV (Department of Motor Vehicle) processes of states thousands of miles away was a legal longshot from Day One."

Louis "Lou" Virelli III, a professor at Stetson University's College of Law in St. Petersburg, came to the same conclusion. "The Supreme Court's docket could be overwhelmed by states suing each other for their policy choices," he said, adding that the high court's 7-2 decision to deny Florida's complaint was "not on the merits, but based on the court's discretionary jurisdiction." Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito cast the two dissenting votes.

Jae Williams, press secretary for the Florida Attorney General's office, issued the following written statement to USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA in response to the Supreme Court's decision: "Unfortunately, the Supreme Court leaves Floridians with no avenue to hold California accountable for putting dangerous, illegal alien truck drivers on our roads, despite the U.S. Constitution's mandate and Congress directing the Court to hear controversies between the states."

The Florida Attorney General's office did not respond to requests for further comment.

Why did Florida go to the Supreme Court to sue California and Washington?

Florida's lawsuit against California and Washington had to do with the two states issuing CDLs to Harjinder Singh, the illegal immigrant truck driver accused of causing the fatal truck crash on Aug. 12, 2025 that killed three people when when he made an illegal U-turn on a crossover marked "Official Use Only" along the Florida's Turnpike near Fort Pierce.

The three Florida residents were killed when the minivan they were riding in collided with Singh's 18-wheel semi-trailer as it was making its U-turn. The Official Use Only sign was accompanied by a universal "No U-turn" symbol.

Singh, 28, is a native of north India of Sikh heritage who entered the United States illegally in 2018 and was issued a CDL from Washington state in 2023 and a non-domiciled CDL from California in 2024. He lives in California.

According to the State of Florida's lawsuit against California and Washington, "State and federal investigations revealed that the illegal immigrant does not speak English. He was able to answer only two of 12 questions correctly on an English proficiency test and identify only one of four traffic signs."

Florida's lawsuit blamed the issuance of CDLs to Singh by California and Washington as resulting in "increasing inspections at state entry points, adding to the workload of both state police and agricultural law enforcement officers."

The lawsuit also urged the Supreme Court to preempt California and Washington's sanctuary laws, which it claimed "prohibit agencies administering CDL programs from inquiring into or collecting information about an applicant's immigration status," as well as to ban the two states from issuing CDLs to applicants who are not U.S. citizens or permanent residents.

Florida in its lawsuit stated that it was presenting its case against California and Washington to the Supreme Court because "no other adequate forum is available for this dispute between separate sovereigns."

In a somewhat unusual move, Uthmeier announced the filing of the lawsuit against California and Washington on the "Hannity" political talk show on Fox News as opposed to the traditional method of holding a press conference.

How did California and Washington react about the claims in Florida's lawsuit?

California and Washington in their legal responses to the Supreme Court both called Florida's lawsuit "unserious" because it failed to show how the their respective CDL programs directly caused the fatal truck crash involving Singh.

Both states also maintained that they follow federal regulations in issuing CDLs, including requiring the ability to read and speak English at a level sufficient to safely operate a commercial vehicle.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta, in his state's legal response, disputed Florida's claim that the Supreme Court was the only available venue to address the matter.

"Florida's complaint focuses on a single car accident — a classic kind of personal injury that private plaintiffs can redress," he wrote. "And any concerns about compliance with federal law can be, and already being, addressed by the FMCSA's review process."

Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown's response to Florida's lawsuit included stating that "Washington law requires CDL applicants to pass written knowledge tests and skills that meet federal standards and prohibits issuance of a CDL unless the applicant is domiciled in Washington and otherwise federally qualified."

Brown added: "Florida lacks standing because it has failed to show an actual harm directly caused by Washington or a remedy this Court could provide that would redress the harm Florida alleges."

Washington state's response to the Supreme Court also listed several instances in which Florida improperly issued CDLs to immigrants with limited English language skills who went on to cause fatal truck crashes.

"The Supreme Court didn't give a reason for its May 26 denial, which is standard practice in such situations," noted Aronberg. "However, Washington's response raised an uncomfortable truth: Florida lives in a glass house on this issue."

California and Washington did revoke CDLs to some immigrants

While California and Washington insist they follow federal standards in issuing CDLs, both states recently canceled a number of licenses issued to immigrants in recent years.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles on March 6 canceled 13,000 non-domiciled CDLs effective immediately per a federal government mandate.

Non-domiciled individuals are those who do not have citizenship or lawful permanent resident status and includes holders of various visas, refugees and asylum seekers.

The California DMV in its press release announcing the cancellations stated that the non-domiciled CDL holders whose licenses got revoked were legally present in the U.S. and met language and safety rules when the licenses were issued.

Washington state's Department of Licensing in December revoked 685 standard CDLs that it acknowledged were issued in error to noncitizens between 2018 and 2025. It also announced a temporary halt in issuing non-domiciled CDLs.

"Errors have been addressed, and DOL is working to make changes in our system ... to prevent mis-issuances in the future," Washington state DOL spokesman Nathan Olson told the regional news website Source One in a Dec. 9 article.

Why are there so many Sikh truckers in the U.S. (including Florida)?

According to some estimates, including The Economist and the India-based news website Firstpost, the number of Sikh truckers in the U.S. may be as many as 135,000 to 150,000.

Gurpatwant Pannun, general counsel for the New York-based Sikhs for Justice organization, believes the number of Sikh truckers in the U.S. is more than 100,000, including "between 3,000 and 5,000" in Florida.

Some are refugees who fled their native homeland in the Punjab region that bisects India and Pakistan to escape religious persecution.

The reason many Sikhs become truckers in the U.S. is because "it allows for entrepreneurial independence while offering flexibility to observe our religious articles of faith, including the turban and beard," wrote Pannun in an email to USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA.

What is Sikhism?

Sikhism is the world's fifth largest organized religion with over 27 million adherents, including an estimated 750,000 in the U.S., according to the New York-based Sikh Coalition. The group states that its religion's core values are love, service and justice and that its followers are easily distinguishable by their uncut hair and wearing of turbans by males.

It is also a religion that is separate from Hinduism and Islam (the dominant religions of India and Pakistan, respectively), with its own places of worship that are called a Gurdwara, or "door of the guru."

Why did Sikhs gather outside a Florida jail?

A small gathering of members of Sikhs for Justice on Aug. 28, 2025 held a "peaceful prayer vigil" outside the St. Lucie County jail where Singh is being held following last year's fatal truck crash.

Pannun who took part in the vigil said it was held to express "deep condolences to the families of the victims," raise funds for the victims' funerals, while "simultaneously standing up" for Harjinder Singh's right to due process.

"Our message is very clear: everyone must get a fair trial," wrote Pannun. "The tragic crash involving Harjinder Singh was an individual case that is currently going through the legal system. It should not be weaponized to restrict industry access (to Sikhs) or to stoke anti-immigrant sentiment."

Pannun added that his organization "supports any legitimate, non-discriminatory measure that improves highway safety for everyone."

That includes the longstanding federal law requiring all CDL holders to have "a working command of the English language," he wrote. "This is not a profession where you can simply bypass safety standards. The reason so many Sikhs enter trucking is due to a strong cultural work ethic, a robust community mentorship network, and the opportunity for economic upward mobility — not a lack of regulations."

How did truckers, Sikh groups react to the Supreme Court's decision?

Armando Reynaldo is an independent trucker based in Hernando County. He doesn't know what to make of the Supreme Court's decision, but agrees something needs to be done to crack down on immigrant truckers who "don't speak English and don't care."

"I know a lot of people who don't speak English good but they understand the laws," said Reynaldo, himself an immigrant from Cuba.

Unfortunately, that's not the case for all immigrant truckers, he said. "I don't know how they got their license. They are a danger. Even in a truck stop, they don't know how to back up their truck. A lot are good, but there's a lot that don't need to be in a truck."

Lewie Pugh is executive vice president of the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association based in the Kansas City, Missouri area. The OOIDA represents more than 150,000 truckers across the U.S. and Canada, including some who are Sikh.

Pugh understands why the Supreme Court elected to not hear Florida's lawsuit against California and Washington. "Florida was trying to fix this in the courts. We feel it's better addressed by the FMCSA (Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration)," he said.

The OOIDA is pushing to establish higher nationwide standards for obtaining a CDL that includes a minimum of 30 hours of behind-the-wheel training, a requirement to read and speak English without the help of a translator, and doing away with non-domiciled CDL programs that allow drivers to train outside their home state and receive a commercial license in a state other than the one they primarily reside in, according to Josh Klein, the association's deputy communications director.

"We are primarily push for these changes through regulations and legislation rather than through the courts," said Pugh.

Pannun praised the Supreme Court decision as "a victory for the rule of law" that "protects thousands of hard-working truck drivers across America. The Court has ensured that states like California and Washington cannot have their licensing systems upended based on a single tragic accident."

Graham West, a spokesman for the New York-based Sikh Coalition, also praised the Supreme Court's decision, but did not characterize it as a victory.

"A successful lawsuit could have had a chilling effect in the willingness of states cross the nation to issue non-domiciled commercial driver's licenses to qualified and lawfully present drivers," he told USA TODAY NETWORK-FLORIDA in an email. "More broadly however, the larger point is somewhat moot given that FMCSA's Final Rule barring most categories of immigrants from obtaining or renewing non-domiciled CDLs is in effect and won't hear its next legal challenge until September."

West was referring to new nationwide FMCSA regulations that took effect March 16.

How the fed's new 'Final Rule' for CDLs accomplishes the aim of Florida's suit

The FMCSA's so-called "Final Rule" limits those eligible to receive a CDL to U.S. citizens and immigrants who are either permanent residents or who hold an H-2A (agricultural worker), H-2B (seasonal non-agricultural worker) or E-2 (treaty investor nation) visa.

No longer eligible are recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) status, refugees and asylum seekers.

"The scope of that exclusion is substantial," according to a March 10 article in the supply chain, transportation and logistics industry trade publication FreightWaves. "FMCSA estimates that 97% of the current 200,000 non-domiciled CDL holders nationwide will not be able to satisfy the new requirements under the Final Rule, assuming it survives legal challenge."

If allowed to stand, the Final Rule could see between 214,000 and 437,000 truckers removed from the workforce nationally over the next two to three years, according to an analysis by Arkansas-based trucking giant J.B. Hunt Transport Services, the FreightWaves article stated.

The Final Rule is being challenged in court by the AFL-CIO, American Federation of Teachers and Public Citizens, the Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit consumer advocacy group founded by Ralph Nader.

"The administrative process worked exactly the way it was supposed to, rendering Florida's lawsuit completely obsolete," said Aronberg. "The federal government has stepped in and is attempting to solve the core safety gap.

"It seems good public policy to have a centralized federal standard that ensures that anyone behind the wheel of an 80,000-pound rig has had their background and driving competency thoroughly vetted. Public safety should always be the primary concern."

He covers everything from insurance, utilities and home prices to groceries, gas and auto prices as the Florida consumer pocketbook reporter. text:
This is one of those everything, everywhere, all at once weeks. There is a lot going on that you need to know about, but most of it is cases or controversies in progress, with no final decision as of yet. It feels more like a Sunday night, where we prepare for the week ahead, than like a Thursday to me in that sense. But I’ll set up some of the most important developments for you here, and we’ll dig in as we get decisions.

Slush fund case-Virginia edition. There is a hearing Friday in the slush fund case in Virginia before Judge Leonie Brinkema in the Eastern District of Virginia. She entered a temporary injunction that kept the fund from going into effect previously, with additional arguments scheduled for tomorrow. After the government argued the case is mooted because they are no longer moving forward, the plaintiffs asked the Judge to let them engage in limited discovery to determine whether the administration has really abandoned its plans to allow the president to dish out taxpayer money to January 6 defendants.

The plaintiffs’ attorneys put it like this: “If the administration truly intends to walk away from this $1.776 billion corrupt political kickback scheme, it should have no problem proving it. Instead, they are asking the court and the public to believe that the fund has been abandoned while the president continues publicly praising the slush fund and refusing to say it has been abandoned. Courts decide cases based on evidence, not shifting political statements. We are seeking discovery to gather facts so the administration can face accountability for one of the most extraordinary abuses of taxpayer funds in modern history.”

Last word on this goes to Representative Jim McGovern, a Democrat, representing Massachusetts’ second district. He said what he said.

Alabama again, this time, over the death penalty. When I originally wrote this section tonight, this matter had not been decided. But around 9:30 p.m. Central, the Supreme Court blocked Alabama’s use of nitrogen gas on a condemned inmate, who was scheduled to be executed Thursday at 6:00 pm. Their decision came on the heels of a Wednesday decision by the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals that the method was unconstitutional. The order states the result—the execution was stayed—but is unsigned and does not include the Court’s reasons. Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Neil Gorsuch noted their dissent and would have granted the state’s request to use this method of execution.

Jeffery Lee, the inmate who was scheduled for execution, challenged the use of nitrogen gas and had asked to be executed by a firing squad. Alabama turned to nitrogen gas in 2024, the first state to do so, as the drugs it used for lethal injections became increasingly difficult to obtain. In this method of execution, an inmate is strapped to a gurney and made to breathe nitrogen gas through a mask apparatus, ultimately depriving them of oxygen and leading to death by asphyxiation. In January of 2024 when it was first used, the Eleventh Circuit declined to interfere, writing that the fact that nitrogen hypoxia is “new and novel” does not mean it is inherently cruel and unusual. But more recently, there have been eyewitness accounts of inhumane suffering, and the American Thoracic Society filed a brief in this case arguing that “nitrogen hypoxia executions cause intense, inhumane suffering.”

The decision does not mean the state cannot execute Lee, who was put on death row by a judge, who overrode a jury’s decision that he should be sentenced to life in prison. That judicial override practice was subsequently ended, but people like Lee who had already but sentenced to death using it did not get any relief.

Cage fighting on the White House Lawn. Today, the White House let the press get a look inside of “The Claw,” where they plan to hold UFC cage fights this Sunday. The New York Times described what they saw like this: “The cage itself was an eight-sided feat of marketeering, its every angle prominently displaying the name of some sponsor who’d paid big bucks to have their brands juxtaposed against the ultimate backdrop: Live Trade on Polymarket … Bud Light … Pit Boss Grills … Total Wireless … Dial #Law Morgan & Morgan … Toyo Tires. The words ‘crypto.com’ were carved into each little metal step leading into the ring.”

In a Reuters and Ipsos poll published today, only 16% of Americans said it was “appropriate” for Mr. Trump to hold the fights on the South Lawn of the White House. But they’ll proceed unless a federal judge says no. The case is fully briefed, and we could get a decision at any moment. The Judge doesn’t have much time left to act, if he’s going to.

The plaintiffs continue to press their suit. Their most recent brief, filed yesterday, argues that the UFC shouldn’t be able to use the Lincoln Memorial chamber and that the court should grant a temporary restraining order to prevent the event from proceeding at all.

They particularly object to a plan they’ve learned of recently that involves closing access to the Lincoln Memorial so the cage fights can proceed.

Meanwhile, the plaintiffs submitted an additional reply to convince the Judge to order halt to the UFC event

They argue that the event, “a volcano of corruption, if allowed to go forward, will mark an inflection point in American history.” They continue, “Unable to defend this spectacle for what it is, Defendants elect to defend something else entirely. They call the event a ‘celebration of the 250th Anniversary of American Independence’ and an ‘official act’ of the President immune from the Court’s scrutiny. But the evidence on display to the American people refutes that story.” It’s a hard argument to beat. As we’ve discussed, it could come down to whether the Judge thinks the plaintiffs have standing.

There are a lot of unanswered questions on this one. If the Judge rules against the government, Trump would almost certainly seek an immediate order from the court of appeals and, if unsuccessful there, go to the Supreme Court. How the district court will rule and whether appellate courts would move quickly enough to permit Trump to go ahead with his birthday plans if the plaintiffs were successful below remains to be seen.

And, like always, there’s a 1984, “Let’s rewrite history” moment tonight. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump has a new gambit to rewrite history. He is “pushing lawmakers to pass a resolution aimed at voiding his first-term impeachments.”

The Journal story assesses the plan like this: “The resolution would allow Trump to claim a symbolic victory on a matter that has dogged him since his first term, part of a broader effort to burnish his presidential legacy. It would have little legal significance, however, because the Constitution provides no procedure for undoing an impeachment, according to experts.” But it shouldn’t be dismissed so easily. This plan is better understood as part of the desperate effort by Trump that we’ve discussed to keep the history books from treating him as the worst president ever.

Reporters at the Journal asked Trump about his plan, and he responded, “It should be done because I did nothing wrong.” He also said, “It was a rigged deal—it was a whole rigged situation.” Of course, nothing could be further from the truth. In both cases, the House found sufficient reason to bring articles of impeachment. In both cases, Republicans in the Senate declined to part ways with the cult and vote to convict. So Trump is wrong, both when he says he did nothing wrong—the evidence speaks for itself—and also when he says the impeachments were rigged, when he was never convicted.

House Speaker Mike Johnson is taking the president’s request seriously. The Journal reported that his comments to them on the plan were “I think it makes a lot of sense the more the evidence comes out, the more we know they really were sham impeachments.” He also said, “We were saying it at the time, now we know. And they make a very compelling case that it should be expunged from the record, because it was a hyperpartisan attack job.”

Sorry, no dice. History will judge, and it should.

All in all, even with some wins, or at least stalemates for the moment, this week, Trump’s Justice Department is losing the fight that really matters in court, the one to maintain its credibility. A Trump appointee to the bench in the Middle District of Florida, Kyle Dudek, is unhappy with the government. He entered a three-page order in Iastrebov v. Warden.

Mr. Iastrebov is in immigration detention. The Judge wrote, “this Court ordered the Government to provide him with an individualized bond hearing,” after the government conceded he was entitled to one. Judge Dudek continued, “What happened next borders on the surreal.”

Here’s what happened: An immigration judge declined to hold the bond hearing. The government didn’t insist on it pursuant to the Judge’s order, though. When the petitioner renewed his motion, the Government, according to Judge Dudek, “casually announces that its previous concession ‘was in error’ and asks this Court to reverse itself and hold that Iastrebov is instead subject to mandatory detention.”

The Judge objects to the government’s disingenuous conduct, finding that it is “not just legally unsupportable, it is a masterclass in litigation cynicism. A federal court is not a testing lab where the Executive branch can pilot a concession to get a case closed, stand by silently while its own administrative process flouts the resulting mandate, and then stroll back in demanding a clean slate. Give me a break.”

But, and here’s the best part, the Judge doesn’t just tell the government to mend its ways. Instead, he ordered the petitioner released from the government’s custody:

“Iastrebov is entitled to a bond hearing. But because the Government has shown a complete inability to follow judicial directions … The Government is directed to release Iastrebov within 48 hours of this Order. Respondents shall facilitate his transportation from the detention facility by notifying his counsel when and where he can be collected.”

And just like that, the government has been bench slapped out of court.

Every day, there's more to track. Slush funds, cage fights on the South Lawn, judges ordering the government to just release someone because they've violated the rules. I'm here every day making sense of it, separating the noise from what actually matters. If you're not already a paid subscriber, joining means you'll be part of a community that takes democracy seriously and makes independent reporting and analysis possible.

We’re in this together,

Joyce
